note: The class version cited FAR 1.108(a) for the meaning of "shall". "Shall denotes the imperative" is a FAR 2.101 definition; the RFO conventions (now FAR 1.107(a)) say Part 2 definitions apply to the whole FAR.
stem: A junior specialist asks whether a FAR sentence that says "shall" is mandatory or optional. What does "shall" mean in the FAR?

options.text: The action is mandatory
options.why: "Shall" denotes the imperative, and "must" means the same (FAR 2.101). The RFO text mostly uses "must".

options.text: The action is preferred but not required
options.why: That is closer to "should": an expected course of action unless inappropriate.

options.text: The action is up to the contractor
options.why: "Shall" is not optional for anyone it is directed at.

options.text: The action is required only when funds are available
options.why: Funding has nothing to do with the meaning of "shall".

note: Same answer as the class version; the RFO moved the FAR conventions from 1.108 to 1.107, so this is now FAR 1.107(a)(2).
stem: You find a word in a clause that is not defined anywhere in that clause, part or Part 2. How do you read it?

options.text: Give it its common dictionary meaning
options.why: Undefined words retain their common dictionary meaning (1.107(a)(2)).

options.text: Borrow a definition from some other part of the FAR
options.why: A definition in a specific part applies only in that part (1.107(a)(1)).

options.text: Write your own definition
options.why: The conventions settle it: dictionary meaning.

options.text: Ignore the word
options.why: Every word counts when reading a clause.

note: The class version asked about "tense and voice" under FAR 1.108(b). That paragraph has always been delegation of authority, and the RFO conventions (FAR 1.107) contain no tense rule. Rewritten to test 1.107(b).
stem: Under the FAR conventions, can an authority the FAR gives to an official be delegated?

options.text: Yes, each authority is delegable unless the FAR specifically says otherwise
options.why: 1.107(b): each authority is delegable unless specifically stated otherwise. That is why the FAR says "not delegable" when it means it, for example competition advocate approval of a justification.

options.text: No, only the agency head may ever exercise a FAR authority
options.why: The FAR pushes decisions to the lowest level consistent with law (1.102(a)(7)).

options.text: Only if the contractor agrees to the delegation in writing
options.why: Delegation is an internal Government matter.

options.text: Only authorities above the SAT can be delegated, and only in writing
options.why: Dollar value has nothing to do with whether an authority is delegable.

note: Same answer as the class version; the rule moved from FAR 1.108(c) to 1.107(c).
stem: A buy is $1 over the simplified acquisition threshold when all options are counted. The contracting officer thinks the $1 is immaterial. How should the threshold be applied?

options.text: Apply it exactly, using the final anticipated value with all options
options.why: A threshold is the final anticipated dollar value of the action, including all options (1.107(c)). Over is over.

options.text: Round down to avoid the extra clauses, since $1 is immaterial
options.why: No rounding is allowed, and splitting or shaving to dodge a threshold is prohibited.

options.text: Use historical prices to ignore the threshold
options.why: History does not change how the threshold is measured.

options.text: Follow agency policy instead of the FAR threshold
options.why: Agency policy cannot override a FAR threshold without a deviation.

note: Same answer as the class version; the rule moved from FAR 1.108(d)(2) to 1.107(d)(2).
stem: Your solicitation went out before a FAR change took effect. When may you include the change in that solicitation?

options.text: If award will happen on or after the change's effective date
options.why: Contracting officers may include FAR changes in earlier solicitations if award occurs on or after the effective date (1.107(d)(2)).

options.text: Only if award happens before the change's effective date
options.why: That is backwards.

options.text: Only if the contractor agrees to the change in writing
options.why: The decision is the contracting officer's for solicitations; consideration matters only for existing contracts (1.107(d)(3)).

options.text: Only if the agency head orders it in a class deviation
options.why: It is at the contracting officer's discretion.

note: Same answer as the class version; the rule moved from FAR 1.108(e) to 1.107(e).
stem: When the FAR cites an OMB circular, what does the citation include?

options.text: All applicable amendments, unless otherwise stated
options.why: Citations to statutes, Executive orders, OMB circulars, OFPP letters and the CFR include all applicable amendments (1.107(e)).

options.text: Only the original version, as first issued
options.why: Amendments are included.

options.text: Only the most recent amendment, if any
options.why: The citation includes all applicable amendments.

options.text: The circular plus every related statute and regulation
options.why: The convention is about amendments to what is cited.

note: Same answer as the class version; the RFO moved this from FAR 1.108(f) "Imperative sentences" to FAR 1.107(f) "Required action".
stem: A FAR sentence directs an action but does not say who does it. Who is responsible?

options.text: The contracting officer
options.why: When a sentence directs action, the contracting officer is responsible unless another party is expressly cited (1.107(f)).

options.text: The contractor, under its clauses
options.why: Contractor duties come from the contract clauses, not FAR directions to the Government.

options.text: The agency head
options.why: The agency head is responsible only when named.

options.text: GAO, as the oversight agency
options.why: GAO decides protests; it does not carry out FAR directions.

note: The class version cited FAR 1.108(d) for deviations. Deviations are in FAR subpart 1.3 under the RFO (they were subpart 1.4 before).
stem: Your technical team wants a clause tailored in a way the FAR does not allow, without asking for a deviation. What is required?

options.text: An approved deviation before you use the inconsistent language
options.why: Using a clause with unauthorized modified language is a deviation (1.301(c)). Individual deviations need agency-head authorization documented in the file (1.303); class deviations follow 1.304.

options.text: Nothing, if the change is minor and the contractor agrees
options.why: The definition has no size exception.

options.text: Legal review only, with a note to the file
options.why: Legal review does not authorize a deviation.

options.text: Tell the contractor but not higher authorities
options.why: Deviations are approved within the Government.

note: The class version described the FAR vision as delivering best value on a timely basis while maintaining public trust and fulfilling public policy (old FAR 1.102(a)). The RFO replaced it with seven guiding principles.
stem: Under the RFO guiding principles, what does the Federal Acquisition Regulations System put first?

options.text: Meeting the agency's mission efficiently and effectively
options.why: 1.102(a)(1). The other principles: effective use of taxpayer dollars that values time, innovation and merit; maximize commercial buying; award to contractors with a superior ability to perform; competition and fair opportunity; integrity, fairness and openness; and decisions at the lowest level.

options.text: Delivering the lowest price in every case
options.why: The principles stress value and mission, not lowest price.

options.text: Eliminating all risk from every acquisition
options.why: The RFO says the System must manage risk, because trying to eliminate all of it is too costly (1.102(c)).

options.text: Requiring Government-unique solutions to fit each need
options.why: The principles say to maximize commercial products and services instead (1.102(a)(3)).

stem: What best describes a contracting officer's role?

options.text: To ensure compliance, and to sign, administer and terminate contracts
options.why: Only contracting officers may sign, administer or terminate contracts (1.402-1). Before signing they make sure all requirements are met and funds are available (1.402-2).

options.text: To give legal advice to contractors about their obligations
options.why: Contracting officers seek legal advice from counsel; they do not advise contractors.

options.text: To oversee only the technical side of a project for the customer
options.why: Technical monitoring is the COR's support role.

options.text: To manage a program's financial accounts and certify the funds
options.why: Resource managers handle accounts and certify funds.

stem: What best describes a federal contracting officer's actual authority?

options.text: Authority delegated in writing through a warrant (SF 1402), with stated limits
options.why: Contracting officers are appointed in writing on an SF 1402 that states limits on their authority (1.403-2(a)), and they bind the Government only within that authority (1.402-1(a)).

options.text: Authority that comes with a job title such as contracting chief
options.why: A title gives no contracting authority.

options.text: Authority from behavior or the common understanding of the office and the contractor
options.why: That is apparent authority, which does not bind the Government.

options.text: Authority delegated orally by a supervisor for urgent buys
options.why: Appointments must be in writing.

stem: Why is apparent authority not recognized in federal contracting?

options.text: Contractors must know that only officials with actual authority can bind the Government
options.why: Anyone dealing with the Government takes the risk of checking the other person's authority. Only actual authority binds; an unauthorized commitment can only be ratified (1.405).

options.text: The Government always has implied liability for the promises its employees make to contractors
options.why: The opposite: without actual authority there is no binding commitment.

options.text: Only military officers in uniform can bind the Government to a contract
options.why: Warranted civilians and enlisted contracting officers bind the Government too.

options.text: Apparent authority applies only to sealed bidding, not to negotiation
options.why: It does not apply in any method.

stem: A program manager tells a contractor to do extra out-of-scope work and promises the contracting officer will approve it later. The contractor does the work and expects payment. What is the Government's obligation?

options.text: Not bound: only a contracting officer can commit, but ratification under 1.405 may be possible
options.why: This is an unauthorized commitment. An official with ratification authority may ratify it if the Government received a benefit, the price is fair and reasonable, funds were and are available, and the other criteria in 1.405(c) are met.

options.text: The Government must pay because the PM had apparent authority over the program
options.why: Apparent authority does not bind the Government.

options.text: The Government must pay because the contractor acted in good faith on the program manager's promise
options.why: Good faith does not create authority.

options.text: The Government must pay only if a funding document was signed before the work
options.why: Funding is not authority to commit.

stem: A new contract specialist issues purchase orders before getting a warrant, saying the branch chief gave permission. Which statement is true?

options.text: The specialist lacks actual authority, and the Government may not be bound
options.why: Contracting officers must be appointed in writing (1.403-2(a)). Orders signed without authority are unauthorized commitments.

options.text: The specialist has apparent authority, so the orders bind the Government
options.why: Apparent authority does not bind the Government.

options.text: Verbal delegation gives actual authority
options.why: Contracting authority must be in writing.

options.text: The branch chief's intent overrides the lack of a warrant
options.why: Intent cannot replace a written appointment.

stem: Your warrant is limited to $1 million. A $1.2 million requirement arrives, and your supervisor tells you to award it today because it is urgent. What do you do?

options.text: Decline and route it to a contracting officer with enough authority
options.why: You can bind the Government only within your warrant's limits (1.402-1(a)).

options.text: Award it because your supervisor directed it in writing and accepts the risk
options.why: A supervisor cannot expand your warrant.

options.text: Cut the quantity to $1 million to fit your warrant
options.why: Changing the requirement to fit your warrant is splitting, not solving.

options.text: Award it now and seek ratification of the excess later
options.why: Knowingly exceeding authority is never a plan.

stem: What is the purpose of a contracting officer's representative (COR)?

options.text: To help monitor performance as designated in writing by the contracting officer
options.why: A COR assists with technical monitoring (1.404(e)) but has no authority to change price, quality, quantity, delivery or other terms (1.404(d)).

options.text: To negotiate contract terms with the contractor's managers
options.why: Only contracting officers negotiate and change terms.

options.text: To manage contract payments and approve the invoices
options.why: Payment is handled by the finance office after acceptance.

options.text: To give legal advice to the contracting officer on disputes, claims and protests
options.why: Legal advice comes from counsel.

stem: A contract specialist evaluating proposals does not disclose that her cousin owns one of the competing companies. What is the main concern?

options.text: A conflict of interest that threatens the impartiality of the evaluation
options.why: Government business must be conducted with complete impartiality and no preferential treatment (3.101-1). She should disclose it and be removed from the evaluation.

options.text: Failure to evaluate the technical factors in the order the RFP stated them
options.why: The problem is her relationship, not her technique.

options.text: Disclosing source selection information to her cousin's firm
options.why: Nothing says she disclosed anything yet.

options.text: Breach of warranty by the cousin's company
options.why: Warranties are contract terms about supplies, not ethics.

stem: A contracting officer obligates funds after being told the appropriation is no longer available because of a lapse. Which Antideficiency Act provision is most directly violated?

options.text: Incurring an obligation in excess or in advance of appropriations
options.why: 31 U.S.C. 1341 forbids obligating more than is available, or before it is available.

options.text: Accepting voluntary services from the contractor
options.why: That is a different ADA prohibition (31 U.S.C. 1342).

options.text: Failing to report a funds shortfall within 30 days
options.why: Reporting comes after a violation; the violation is the obligation.

options.text: Paying an invoice without a certified receiving report from the COR
options.why: That is a payment-process problem, not the ADA violation described.

stem: A program office over-obligated funds because a modification was processed without checking fund availability. What reporting does an Antideficiency Act violation require?

options.text: Report it immediately through the agency head to the President and Congress
options.why: 31 U.S.C. 1351 requires the agency head to report all relevant facts and actions taken immediately to the President and Congress.

options.text: Tell the contractor and withhold payment until replacement funds are found
options.why: The contractor's payment is not the remedy for an internal violation.

options.text: Notify GAO and the contractor within 60 days of finding it
options.why: That is not the statutory reporting chain.

options.text: Quietly deobligate the excess to fix it without reporting
options.why: Fixing the numbers does not remove the duty to report.

note: The class version cited the Truthful Cost or Pricing Data threshold as $2 million. It is now $2.5 million under the FAR (15.403-3) and, for DoW prime contracts awarded after 30 June 2026, $10 million (FY2026 NDAA; DFARS 215.403-3 class deviation).
stem: In November 2026 you are negotiating a $3 million DoW sole-source contract. No exception applies. Must the contractor submit certified cost or pricing data?

options.text: No: DoW's threshold is $10 million after 30 June 2026, though you may request other data
options.why: The FY2026 NDAA raised DoW's threshold to $10 million. Below it, request only the data other than certified cost or pricing data you need (15.403-1).

options.text: Yes, because $3 million is above the $2 million FAR threshold for certified data
options.why: $2 million is outdated: the FAR figure is $2.5 million, and DoW's is now $10 million.

options.text: Yes, for every firm-fixed-price sole-source contract above the SAT
options.why: Contract type does not trigger certified data.

options.text: Only if it is competitive and over $10 million in total value
options.why: Adequate price competition is an exception: competitive awards normally do not need certified data.

stem: When must certified cost or pricing data NOT be obtained?

options.text: At or below the SAT, or when an exception applies, such as adequate price competition
options.why: Certified data must not be obtained at or below the SAT (15.403-2(a)) or when an exception applies (15.403-2(b)): adequate price competition, prices set by law, commercial items, or a waiver.

options.text: Whenever the contract is cost-reimbursement, because costs are audited later anyway
options.why: Cost-type contracts often need certified data.

options.text: Whenever the contractor objects to giving the data in writing
options.why: Contractor preference is not an exception.

options.text: Only on construction contracts, whatever their value
options.why: No construction exception exists.

stem: When are prices based on adequate price competition in DoW?

options.text: Two or more responsible offerors compete independently, price is a substantial factor, and the price is not unreasonable
options.why: 15.403-2(c)(1)(i). The one-offer path in (c)(1)(ii) does not apply to DoW, which also resolicits when only one offer comes in (DFARS 215.371).

options.text: Only one offer is received, but the contracting officer reasonably expected real competition when the solicitation was issued
options.why: That path is for agencies other than DoW, NASA and the Coast Guard.

options.text: The IGCE matches the price within ten percent and the offeror is responsible
options.why: An IGCE comparison is a price analysis technique, not adequate price competition.

options.text: The offer comes from a small business that competed in a set-aside with one offer
options.why: Size status has nothing to do with it.

stem: You are preparing to negotiate a $25 million DoW sole-source contract and look up the contractor in the Contract Business Analysis Repository (CBAR). What is CBAR mainly for?

options.text: Finding data on contractors, such as business system status, rates and other DoW negotiations
options.why: CBAR, run by DCMA, gives contracting officers data on contractors and negotiations completed by DoW procuring contracting officers, which helps you prepare.

options.text: Tracking contractor performance ratings and comments for use in DoW source selections
options.why: Performance ratings are in CPARS.

options.text: Submitting invoices for audit before payment by DFAS
options.why: Invoices go through PIEE (WAWF).

options.text: Reporting procurement integrity violations to the Inspector General
options.why: Violations go to the chain and the HCA (3.104-7), not CBAR.

note: The class version cited FAR 5.202 and 5.203 for exceptions and response times. Under the RFO, presolicitation notice exemptions are in FAR 5.101(b) and times are in Tables 5-2 and 5-3.
stem: You will award a $5 million contract sole-source under the only-one-responsible-source exception. What does Part 5 require for notices?

options.text: Post a notice unless another exemption applies; sole source alone does not exempt it
options.why: Using other than full and open competition exempts you from the notice EXCEPT for 6.103-1 (only one source) and 6.103-6 (national security) (5.101(b)(2)). Posting may find another source.

options.text: Skip notices, because a sole-source award has only one possible offeror
options.why: That is exactly the case the RFO still requires a notice for.

options.text: Notify only small businesses and internal stakeholders by email
options.why: Notices go to the GPE (SAM.gov) for everyone.

options.text: Post only the justification after award, which replaces the presolicitation notice
options.why: The justification is posted after award (6.301), but the presolicitation notice is still required here.

note: The class version used $350,000. Under the RFO, actions at or below the SAT need no separate presolicitation notice when the solicitation itself is posted on SAM.gov with electronic responses (FAR 5.101(b)(1)(i)), so the example now uses a value above the SAT.
stem: You will solicit a $500,000 noncommercial supply requirement. What must you do under Part 5?

options.text: Post a notice 15 days before the solicitation, then allow at least 30 days for offers
options.why: Above the SAT, noncommercial buys need a notice 15 days before the solicitation (Table 5-2) and at least 30 days from the solicitation to receive offers (Table 5-3): about 45 days from notice to closing.

options.text: No notice, because $500,000 is under the simplified acquisition threshold for supplies
options.why: $500,000 is above the $350,000 SAT.

options.text: Post it on the contractor's website and the agency's social media
options.why: Notices go to the Governmentwide point of entry, SAM.gov.

options.text: Post only if market research found fewer than three sources
options.why: The notice rule does not depend on how many sources exist.

note: The class version said to shorten the synopsis time under FAR 5.203. Under the RFO, using the urgency exception (6.103-2) exempts you from the presolicitation notice (FAR 5.101(b)(2)), and the justification is posted within 30 days after award (FAR 6.301(b)(1)).
stem: After a hurricane you must award a disaster recovery contract within 3 days using the unusual and compelling urgency exception. What does Part 5 require?

options.text: Skip the notice, but document urgency, solicit as many sources as practicable, and post the J&A
options.why: Urgency is an other-than-full-and-open authority that is exempt from the notice (5.101(b)(2)). Its justification may follow award (6.103-2(d)) and is posted within 30 days (6.301(b)(1)).

options.text: Skip all publicizing and documentation entirely, since disaster buys are exempt from Part 5
options.why: The justification and its posting are still required.

options.text: Post a special notice only after award, explaining the hurricane
options.why: Special notices are not the urgency mechanism.

options.text: Wait 15 days for the notice period before soliciting any offers
options.why: The urgency exemption removes the notice requirement.

note: The class version cited FAR 5.202 and offered old section numbers as choices. Under the RFO the national security exemption is FAR 5.101(b)(1)(ii).
stem: Describing a classified intelligence support requirement in a notice would compromise national security. Which RFO rule lets you skip the presolicitation notice?

options.text: The 5.101(b) exemption for notices that would compromise national security
options.why: 5.101(b)(1)(ii) exempts these actions. The related competition exception is national security (6.103-6).

options.text: The 10-day posting rule for proposed actions valued between $20,000 and $25,000
options.why: That sets a posting time, not an exemption.

options.text: Paid advertisement rules for classified buys
options.why: 5.102 covers optional paid advertisements.

options.text: Requests from small businesses for copies of the solicitation
options.why: 5.202 covers giving solicitation copies to small businesses on request.

note: The class version asked whether an award notice is due in 14 or 30 days under FAR 5.301. The RFO sets no fixed day count for this case: post as soon as possible if subcontracting is likely, or within 60 days if only trade agreements apply (Table 5-4).
stem: You awarded a $12 million firm-fixed-price contract that is likely to produce subcontracts. What award notice do you post on SAM.gov?

options.text: An award notice, posted as soon as possible after award
options.why: Award notices are required over $25,000 for actions likely to result in subcontracts or covered by trade agreements; when subcontracts are likely, post as soon as possible (5.301(d)).

options.text: Nothing, because it was competed in the open
options.why: Competition does not exempt an award notice.

options.text: Notify only the unsuccessful offerors
options.why: Offeror notices are separate (15.207-2); the public award notice is still required.

options.text: Post within 60 days in every case, with the price and the winner's name
options.why: 60 days applies when subcontracts are not likely and only trade agreements require the notice.

stem: What does the Uniform Contract Format (UCF) mainly do?

options.text: Standardizes how solicitations and contracts are organized (sections A to M)
options.why: The UCF puts the same information in the same place every time: Part I the Schedule (A-H), Part II clauses (I), Part III attachments (J) and Part IV representations and instructions (K-M).

options.text: Sets the evaluation criteria for every negotiated buy
options.why: Evaluation factors are one section (M) of the UCF.

options.text: Defines the performance standards and the inspection rules for service contracts
options.why: Those go in Section C and the PWS.

options.text: Establishes the contract terms and the prices for each line
options.why: Terms go in the sections; the format just organizes them.

note: The class version said the UCF is required under old FAR 14.201-1 and 15.204-1. Under the RFO, IFBs use it "to the maximum practicable extent" (FAR 14.201-1(a)) and RFPs "should" use it (FAR 15.102(b)(1)), with listed exceptions such as construction.
stem: Under the RFO, when should a contracting officer use the Uniform Contract Format?

options.text: For IFBs and RFPs, with exceptions such as construction and streamlined RFPs
options.why: IFBs use the UCF to the maximum practicable extent (14.201-1(a)); RFPs should use it (15.102(b)(1)), except construction, A-E, subsistence, special formats, streamlined RFPs and agency-exempted buys (15.102(b)(2)).

options.text: Only for purchase orders under simplified procedures
options.why: Purchase orders use simple forms such as the SF 1449, OF 347 or DD 1155.

options.text: Only for major systems and other buys over $100 million that need formal source selection
options.why: It is the default for negotiated and sealed-bid contracts, not just major systems.

options.text: Never; the RFO eliminated it for all contracts
options.why: The RFO kept the UCF (15.109).

stem: Which UCF section gives instructions, conditions and notices to offerors?

options.text: Section L
options.why: Section L tells offerors how to prepare proposals. Section M says how they will be evaluated; the two must line up.

options.text: Section B
options.why: Section B is Supplies or Services and Prices/Costs.

options.text: Section C
options.why: Section C is the description, specifications or work statement.

options.text: Section M
options.why: Section M is Evaluation Factors for Award.

stem: Where in the UCF do you find the statement of work or performance work statement?

options.text: Section C
options.why: Section C, Description/Specifications/Statement of Work (requirements).

options.text: Section F
options.why: Section F is Deliveries or Performance.

options.text: Section H
options.why: Section H is Special Contract Requirements.

options.text: Section L
options.why: Section L is Instructions to Offerors.

stem: Which UCF section holds the evaluation factors for award?

options.text: Section M
options.why: Section M lists the factors, significant subfactors and their relative importance.

options.text: Section J
options.why: Section J is the List of Attachments.

options.text: Section L
options.why: Section L is the instructions.

options.text: Section B
options.why: Section B is the supplies or services and prices.

stem: Where are the contract clauses in the UCF?

options.text: Section I (Part II)
options.why: Part II, Section I, Contract Clauses.

options.text: Section C (Part I)
options.why: Section C is the requirement.

options.text: Section L (Part IV)
options.why: Section L holds solicitation provisions for offerors.

options.text: Section K (Part IV)
options.why: Section K holds representations and certifications.

stem: Which UCF section contains the representations, certifications and other statements of offerors?

options.text: Section K
options.why: Section K holds the provisions that require representations and certifications.

options.text: Section G
options.why: Section G is Contract Administration Data.

options.text: Section J
options.why: Section J is the List of Attachments.

options.text: Section H
options.why: Section H is Special Contract Requirements.

note: The class version asked which section is "not always physically included but may be referenced" and offered B, J, M and I, none of which fits well. The RFO says Part IV (K, L, M) is not physically included and Section K is incorporated by reference (FAR 15.109, 14.307(e)(3)).
stem: At award, which UCF section is not physically included in the contract but is incorporated by reference?

options.text: Section K, Representations and certifications
options.why: Part IV (K, L and M) stays in the contract file, not the contract; Section K is incorporated by reference through clauses such as 52.204-19 (15.109).

options.text: Section B, Supplies or Services and Prices/Costs
options.why: Section B is the heart of the contract and is always included.

options.text: Section I, Contract Clauses (Part II)
options.why: Section I is part of the contract.

options.text: Section M, Evaluation Factors for Award
options.why: Section M is not physically included, but it is not incorporated by reference either; it simply has no role after award.

stem: What goes in Section B of the UCF?

options.text: The supplies or services and their prices (the line items)
options.why: Section B lists the contract line items (CLINs) with quantities and prices.

options.text: The statement of work and the delivery schedule
options.why: That is Section C.

options.text: Evaluation criteria and their relative importance for award
options.why: That is Section M.

options.text: Special contract requirements for the work
options.why: That is Section H.

stem: Which UCF section covers delivery or performance schedules?

options.text: Section F
options.why: Section F, Deliveries or Performance: time, place and method.

options.text: Section C
options.why: Section C is the requirement.

options.text: Section E
options.why: Section E is Inspection and Acceptance.

options.text: Section G
options.why: Section G is Contract Administration Data.

stem: Where in the UCF are attachments such as technical exhibits and data requirements listed?

options.text: Section J (Part III)
options.why: Section J lists every attached document, exhibit and attachment.

options.text: Section G (Part I)
options.why: Section G is administration data.

options.text: Section H (Part I)
options.why: Section H is special requirements.

options.text: Section L (Part IV)
options.why: Section L is instructions to offerors.

stem: Which UCF section usually holds payment instructions and accounting data?

options.text: Section G, Contract Administration Data
options.why: Section G holds accounting and appropriation data and administration instructions, including payment information.

options.text: Section B, Supplies or Services and Prices
options.why: Section B has the prices, not payment instructions.

options.text: Section C, Description/Specifications
options.why: Section C is the requirement.

options.text: Section F, Deliveries or Performance
options.why: Section F is delivery.

stem: Where in the UCF are inspection and acceptance requirements?

options.text: Section E
options.why: Section E, Inspection and Acceptance, includes quality assurance and reliability requirements.

options.text: Section A
options.why: Section A is the solicitation/contract form.

options.text: Section C
options.why: Section C is the requirement.

options.text: Section L
options.why: Section L is the instructions.

stem: What is a solicitation provision?

options.text: A term used only in solicitations that applies only before award
options.why: Provisions apply before award; clauses apply after award, or both before and after (2.101).

options.text: A term that applies only after award, during contract performance
options.why: That describes a clause.

options.text: A requirement written into the awarded contract
options.why: Contract requirements are clauses.

options.text: A general policy for all acquisitions in the agency
options.why: Policy is in the FAR text, not provisions.

stem: A term or condition affects both the solicitation and the resulting contract. What is it, and where does it appear?

options.text: A clause, and it appears in both the solicitation and the contract
options.why: A clause is used in contracts, or in both solicitations and contracts, and applies after award or both before and after (2.101).

options.text: A provision, kept only in Section K of the contract
options.why: Provisions apply only before award.

options.text: A provision that becomes a clause at award
options.why: Provisions do not convert into clauses.

options.text: A clause incorporated only after award, by a bilateral modification
options.why: Offerors need to see clauses in the solicitation to price them.

stem: Why is 52.212-1, Instructions to Offerors, a provision and not a clause?

options.text: It applies only during the solicitation phase
options.why: It tells offerors how to respond, which matters only before award.

options.text: It applies only after award, during performance
options.why: That would make it a clause.

options.text: It governs contractor performance
options.why: Performance is governed by clauses such as 52.212-4.

options.text: It contains post-award remedies
options.why: Remedies are in clauses.

stem: Why is 52.232-1, Payments, in the contract rather than only in the solicitation instructions?

options.text: It is a clause that governs contract performance after award
options.why: Payment terms apply after award, so it is a clause.

options.text: It is a provision that offerors must sign
options.why: Provisions apply only before award.

options.text: It matters only before award, for pricing
options.why: Payment happens after award.

options.text: It is optional in fixed-price contracts over the simplified acquisition threshold
options.why: It is prescribed for fixed-price supply and service contracts.

note: The class version said the DFARS supplements the FAR. The fuller answer, taught in CON 1100 and confirmed by the RFO's FAR 1.201, is that agency regulations implement or supplement the FAR.
stem: What is the purpose of the Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (DFARS)?

options.text: To implement and supplement the FAR with defense-specific rules
options.why: Agency regulations implement the FAR (more detail on a FAR topic) or supplement it (topics the FAR does not cover) (1.201(a)(1)). They may not repeat or conflict with the FAR (1.201(a)(2)).

options.text: To replace the FAR for DoW contracting offices
options.why: The DFARS works alongside the FAR, never instead of it.

options.text: To give guidance on international buys only
options.why: The DFARS covers far more than foreign acquisition.

options.text: To simplify buying from small businesses in DoW by raising the thresholds
options.why: That is not its purpose.

stem: Which form is used to modify a contract or amend a solicitation?

options.text: SF 30, Amendment of Solicitation/Modification of Contract
options.why: The SF 30 is used for amendments, change orders, administrative changes, supplemental agreements and funding actions (43.401(a)).

options.text: SF 1449, Solicitation/Contract/Order for Commercial Products
options.why: The SF 1449 is the commercial solicitation/contract/order form.

options.text: DD 1155, Order for Supplies or Services
options.why: The DD 1155 is DoW's order for supplies or services.

options.text: SF 1442, Solicitation, Offer, and Award (Construction)
options.why: The SF 1442 is the construction solicitation, offer and award.

note: Same answer as the class version; the RFO title is Solicitation/Contract/Order for Commercial Products and Commercial Services.
stem: What is the SF 1449 used for?

options.text: Solicitation, contract and order for commercial products and services
options.why: The SF 1449 is used for commercial RFQs, purchase orders and contracts (12.201-1(c)(1), 12.204(c)).

options.text: A request for proposals for noncommercial work
options.why: Noncommercial RFPs use the SF 33, OF 308 or no prescribed form.

options.text: A small business subcontracting plan submitted by large prime contractors
options.why: Subcontracting plans are not on a standard form.

options.text: A contract modification for commercial contracts
options.why: Modifications use the SF 30.

note: The class version offered four wrong answers (bid sample, subcontracting plan, modification, waiver). The SF 1442 is the Solicitation, Offer, and Award form for construction, alteration or repair.
stem: Which form is the solicitation, offer and award form for construction?

options.text: SF 1442, Solicitation, Offer, and Award (Construction)
options.why: Construction solicitations and awards use the SF 1442.

options.text: SF 30, Amendment of Solicitation/Modification of Contract
options.why: The SF 30 amends solicitations and modifies contracts.

options.text: SF 1449, Solicitation/Contract/Order for Commercial Products
options.why: The SF 1449 is for commercial products and services.

options.text: SF 44, Purchase Order-Invoice-Voucher
options.why: The SF 44 is a pocket purchase order for over-the-counter micro-purchases.

stem: What is a procurement instrument identifier (PIID)?

options.text: A Governmentwide-unique number for each solicitation, contract, agreement or order
options.why: The PIID is used on all related actions and forms (4.201(a)). Modifications and amendments get a separate supplementary number.

options.text: A document describing the technical requirement, its standards and the delivery schedule
options.why: That is the SOW or PWS.

options.text: A list of the data deliverables and their due dates
options.why: That is the contract data requirements list.

options.text: A plan for evaluating contractor performance during the contract
options.why: That is a QASP.

note: Same answer as the class version. Under RFO FAR 4.201(b) a PIID is 13 to 17 characters with no hyphens; the hyphens below are only for reading.
stem: Look at the PIID W911S8-23-D-0123. What type of instrument is it?

options.text: An indefinite-delivery contract
options.why: Position 9 is the instrument type, and D is an indefinite-delivery contract (Table 4-1).

options.text: A blanket purchase agreement
options.why: BPAs use A.

options.text: A lease agreement for equipment
options.why: Leases use L.

options.text: A request for quotations
options.why: RFQs use Q.

stem: Look at the PIID W911S8-23-A-0123. What type of instrument is it?

options.text: A blanket purchase agreement
options.why: A in position 9 means a BPA.

options.text: A contract (other than indefinite-delivery)
options.why: Contracts other than indefinite-delivery use C.

options.text: A grant to a university
options.why: Grants are not procurement instruments and have no PIID letter.

options.text: A cooperative agreement
options.why: Cooperative agreements are not procurement instruments.

stem: Look at the PIID W911S8-27-C-2123. What type of instrument is it?

options.text: A contract (of any type except indefinite-delivery)
options.why: C in position 9 means a contract other than an indefinite-delivery contract.

options.text: A grant or other assistance instrument
options.why: Grants have no PIID letter.

options.text: A cooperative agreement with a nonprofit
options.why: Not a procurement instrument.

options.text: An interagency agreement with another Government office
options.why: Not identified by C.

stem: Look at the PIID W911XX-19-B-0123. What type of instrument is it?

options.text: An invitation for bids
options.why: B in position 9 means an IFB.

options.text: A contract
options.why: Contracts use C.

options.text: A basic ordering agreement
options.why: BOAs use G.

options.text: A grant
options.why: Grants have no PIID letter.

stem: What does the W911NF at the start of a PIID tell you?

options.text: The issuing office's activity address code (agency and office)
options.why: Positions 1 to 6 are the issuing office's Activity Address Code (4.201(b)(1)). Positions 7 and 8 are the fiscal year, 9 the instrument type, then the serial number.

options.text: That it is a grant from the Army research office
options.why: The first six characters identify the office, not the instrument.

options.text: The instrument type and the fiscal year
options.why: The type is position 9.

options.text: That it is a purchase order issued under the simplified procedures
options.why: Purchase orders are P in position 9.

stem: What is a bilateral modification?

options.text: A modification signed by both the contractor and the contracting officer
options.why: Bilateral modifications make negotiated equitable adjustments, definitize letter contracts and reflect other agreements of the parties (43.203(a)).

options.text: A modification made without the contractor's consent
options.why: That is unilateral.

options.text: A modification that changes only the price and nothing else in the contract
options.why: A bilateral modification can change any term both parties agree to.

options.text: A modification that extends the period of performance
options.why: Extensions can be bilateral or, through an option, unilateral.

stem: After award, the quantity is increased and both the contractor and the contracting officer sign the document. What kind of action is this?

options.text: A bilateral modification
options.why: Signed by both parties: a supplemental agreement.

options.text: A solicitation amendment
options.why: Amendments change solicitations, not awarded contracts.

options.text: A unilateral modification
options.why: Unilateral modifications are signed only by the contracting officer.

options.text: A change order
options.why: A change order is unilateral.

stem: You must update the paying office and fix a clerical error in the contract number. Price and performance are not affected. Which modification and form do you use?

options.text: An administrative change, issued as a unilateral SF 30
options.why: An administrative change does not affect the parties' substantive rights (43.201) and is issued unilaterally on an SF 30 (43.203(b)(1), 43.401(a)(1)(iv)).

options.text: A substantive bilateral SF 30 signed by both parties
options.why: No substantive right changes, so no agreement is needed.

options.text: A unilateral change order on an SF 1449
options.why: Change orders are under the Changes clause; the form is the SF 30.

options.text: A supplemental agreement on contractor letterhead
options.why: Modifications are issued on the SF 30, not letterhead.

stem: You need to update the paying office address. No contractor signature is needed. Which modification do you issue?

options.text: A unilateral modification
options.why: Administrative changes are unilateral (43.203(b)(1)).

options.text: A bilateral modification
options.why: No agreement is needed for an administrative change.

options.text: A change order
options.why: A change order changes the work under the Changes clause.

options.text: A solicitation amendment
options.why: The contract is already awarded.

stem: Which scenario calls for a unilateral modification?

options.text: A change order issued under the Changes clause
options.why: Change orders, administrative changes, changes under other clauses (options, property, suspension of work) and termination notices are unilateral (43.203(b)).

options.text: A negotiated price adjustment signed by both parties
options.why: Signed by both: bilateral.

options.text: A subcontractor change the contractor initiated
options.why: Contractor-initiated changes need agreement or consent.

options.text: Adding new work by mutual agreement
options.why: Mutual agreement: bilateral.

stem: Which of these requires a bilateral modification?

options.text: A supplemental agreement to revise delivery dates
options.why: Changing delivery dates by agreement is a supplemental agreement, signed by both parties.

options.text: Exercising an option the Government holds
options.why: Options are exercised unilaterally under the option clause.

options.text: A change order under the Changes clause for new work
options.why: The change order is unilateral; only the later equitable adjustment is bilateral.

options.text: Correcting a typographical error
options.why: That is an administrative change, unilateral.

stem: A contractor falls behind because of unforeseen technical problems and asks for more time. What is the best course of action?

options.text: If justified, revise the schedule by bilateral modification, with consideration if the contractor is at fault
options.why: A schedule change by agreement is a supplemental agreement. If the delay is not excusable, the Government should get consideration for giving up its right to on-time delivery.

options.text: Deny it and terminate for default immediately to protect the Government
options.why: Default needs a careful review of the facts and remedies first (49.402-3(a)).

options.text: Approve it informally by email, since a schedule change does not need a modification
options.why: An informal extension can waive the Government's rights; put it in a modification.

options.text: Let the contractor keep working, and deal with the late schedule and any damages at the very end of the contract
options.why: Ignoring the delay can waive the delivery date.

note: Same answer as the class version; the RFO moved the scope rule for change orders to FAR 43.301(a).
stem: You issue a change order to relocate electrical conduits in a building under construction. The contractor says the change is so big it alters the original deal. What must you assess?

options.text: Whether the change is within the scope of the original contract
options.why: The Changes clause allows unilateral changes only within the contract's scope (43.301(a)). Work outside the scope is new work that needs competition or a justification.

options.text: Whether the contractor is legally obligated to comply
options.why: If the change is in scope the contractor must proceed (43.301(b)); the first question is scope.

options.text: Whether the contractor waived its right to protest
options.why: Protests concern awards, not contract changes.

options.text: Whether the price increase exceeds the micro-purchase threshold
options.why: Dollar size alone does not decide scope.

note: Same answer as the class version; the cite moved from FAR 43.204 to 43.304(b) and 43.203(a)(1).
stem: After you issue a change order, the contractor sends a detailed request for an equitable adjustment in price and time. What is your next step?

options.text: Negotiate the adjustment and definitize it with a supplemental agreement
options.why: Negotiate equitable adjustments from change orders in the shortest practicable time (43.304(b)) and record them in a bilateral modification (43.203(a)(1)) with a release (43.304(c)).

options.text: Deny it unless the contractor proves the Government was at fault for the change
options.why: A change order you issued entitles the contractor to an equitable adjustment for its effects.

options.text: Issue a unilateral modification closing the contract
options.why: The adjustment must be negotiated first.

options.text: Send it to legal counsel and wait for their decision
options.why: Counsel can help, but negotiating is your job.

note: The class version said to process the request as a constructive change and evaluate it. A QAR has no authority to change the contract, so the clearer answer is that it is an unauthorized commitment that may be ratified under FAR 1.405 if the criteria are met. The contractor also should have told the contracting officer (FAR 43.204).
stem: A quality assurance representative, who is not a contracting officer, insisted the contractor use a more expensive brand than the contract specified. The contractor did, and now asks for the cost difference. What do you do?

options.text: Review the facts: the QAR lacked authority, so treat it as a possible unauthorized commitment for ratification
options.why: Only contracting officers may change contracts (43.202(a)). Contractors should notify the Government of unwritten changes (43.204). A proper ratification lets you pay a fair price for a benefit the Government received.

options.text: Pay it automatically, because a Government employee directed the change
options.why: Direction by someone without authority does not bind the Government.

options.text: Deny it without reviewing the facts, since only a contracting officer can ever change the terms of the contract
options.why: You must look at the facts; ratification may be appropriate.

options.text: Tell the contractor to settle it with the QAR, who made the decision
options.why: The QAR cannot pay or change anything.

stem: You issue a final decision denying a contractor's claim for added labor costs from a Government delay. The contractor disagrees. What are its options?

options.text: Appeal to the board within 90 days, or sue in the Court of Federal Claims within 12 months
options.why: Both deadlines run from receipt of the final decision, and the decision itself must say so. For DoW the board is the ASBCA.

options.text: Protest to GAO within 10 days of the final decision
options.why: GAO decides bid protests, not contract claims.

options.text: Sue in a U.S. District Court within 60 days, or ask GAO to review the decision
options.why: District courts do not hear Contract Disputes Act claims.

options.text: Resubmit the claim with new evidence within 30 days, or ask the board for mediation before deciding
options.why: A final decision is appealed, not resubmitted.

note: Same answer as the class version; the cites moved from FAR 33.206 and 33.207 to 33.205 and clause 52.233-1.
stem: On a DoW construction contract the contractor hits unexpected rock not shown in the plans. The contracting officer refuses a modification, so the contractor submits a certified claim over $100,000 under the Differing Site Conditions clause. What happens next?

options.text: The CO must decide within 60 days or set a decision date, and the contractor keeps working
options.why: For claims over $100,000, decide within 60 days of receiving the certified claim or say when you will (33.205-6). The Disputes clause requires the contractor to proceed diligently pending resolution.

options.text: The contractor must stop work until the claim is resolved by the board
options.why: The contractor must keep performing.

options.text: The contractor should go straight to the Court of Federal Claims without filing a claim first
options.why: A claim and a final decision (or deemed denial) come first.

options.text: The claim is invalid unless it was filed within 60 days of discovering the rock
options.why: Claims may be filed within 6 years of accrual; the clause's prompt-notice rule is separate.

stem: To whom can a contractor submit a bid protest?

options.text: The agency, GAO, or the Court of Federal Claims
options.why: The three protest forums. Subpart 33.1 covers agency and GAO protests; the Court of Federal Claims follows its own rules (33.106).

options.text: DCMA, which administers the contract
options.why: DCMA administers contracts; it does not decide protests.

options.text: The Small Business Administration or the agency
options.why: SBA decides size and status protests, not bid protests generally.

options.text: OMB, through the agency's budget office
options.why: OMB does not decide protests.

stem: What is GAO's role in the acquisition process?

options.text: To review and decide bid protests
options.why: GAO decides protests under 4 CFR part 21, generally within 100 days.

options.text: To give legal advice to contracting officers
options.why: Agency counsel advises contracting officers.

options.text: To oversee contract performance
options.why: That is the contracting officer, COR and DCMA.

options.text: To manage contract payments
options.why: Finance offices pay contracts.

stem: What is the role of the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA)?

options.text: To administer contracts delegated to it, overseeing performance and compliance
options.why: Contracting officers can delegate contract administration functions to a contract administration office such as DCMA (42.202, 42.302).

options.text: To give legal advice to the contracting officer on claims
options.why: Counsel gives legal advice.

options.text: To make contract payments to the contractors after the receiving report is signed
options.why: DFAS and other finance offices pay.

options.text: To do market research for the requiring activities
options.why: Market research is done by the acquisition team before solicitation.

stem: Which is a key part of contract administration?

options.text: Monitoring contractor performance
options.why: Contract administration means making sure the contractor delivers what the contract says, on time and to standard.

options.text: Conducting market research
options.why: That is pre-award planning.

options.text: Evaluating proposals
options.why: That is source selection, before award.

options.text: Writing the statement of work
options.why: That is requirement development, before solicitation.

stem: A contract is complete. Who is primarily responsible for making sure the contractor's performance evaluation in CPARS is done on time?

options.text: The contracting officer or the assessing official the agency designates
options.why: Agencies assign evaluation roles (42.1103(a)); evaluations are due at least annually and when the work is complete (42.1102(a)).

options.text: The contractor, who drafts its own evaluation
options.why: The contractor comments on the evaluation; it does not write it.

options.text: The program manager alone, as the customer
options.why: The PM gives input, but the assigned official is responsible.

options.text: Nobody; CPARS evaluations are optional once the contract has been completed
options.why: Evaluations are required above the SAT (42.1102(b)).

stem: In a new services source selection, what role does CPARS play in evaluating past performance?

options.text: It is the official Governmentwide source of contractor past performance
options.why: CPARS is the official source for past performance information (42.1101(b)); evaluators also use information from other sources (15.202(c)(3)).

options.text: It is where offerors upload their customer testimonials and performance awards
options.why: Ratings come from Government assessing officials.

options.text: It gives independent cost analyses of each offeror's rates
options.why: Cost analysis comes from your team and DCAA.

options.text: It verifies subcontractor payment history only, for primes
options.why: Payment behavior is one element; CPARS covers all performance.

stem: Which is a key part of contract closeout?

options.text: Confirming all contract terms are met and all administrative actions are done
options.why: Closeout verifies the checklist in 4.308-1(a) and ends with a contract completion statement (4.308-1(b)).

options.text: Conducting market research for the follow-on contract so there is no gap in service
options.why: Pre-award.

options.text: Evaluating proposals for the next requirement
options.why: Pre-award.

options.text: Writing the statement of work for the replacement contract
options.why: Pre-award.

stem: All deliverables were accepted, but the contractor has not sent its final invoice 90 days after the period of performance ended. What should the contracting officer do?

options.text: Start closeout and document the attempts to get the final invoice
options.why: Closeout starts once there is evidence of physical completion (4.308-2(a)). Follow up with the contractor, document every attempt, and follow your agency's closeout procedures (DFARS and PGI) for a contractor that does not submit a final invoice.

options.text: Deobligate the remaining funds and close the contract without any follow-up
options.why: Excess funds are deobligated as part of closeout, after the required checks and contacts.

options.text: Wait for the invoice indefinitely
options.why: Closeout has time standards (Table 4-2).

options.text: Issue a cure notice for the missing invoice
options.why: Cure notices address performance failures before default, not paperwork after completion.

stem: What is a firm-fixed-price contract?

options.text: A contract that pays a set price whatever the contractor's actual costs
options.why: The contractor carries maximum cost risk and full responsibility for costs and profit or loss (16.202-1).

options.text: A contract that pays the actual costs incurred plus a fixed fee for the contractor
options.why: That is cost-reimbursement.

options.text: A contract that reimburses all allowable costs
options.why: That is cost-reimbursement.

options.text: A contract that pays based on outcomes measured each month
options.why: Outcome-based features belong to incentive or performance-based arrangements.

stem: Which of these is a cost-reimbursement contract type?

options.text: Cost-plus-fixed-fee (CPFF)
options.why: CPFF reimburses allowable costs and pays a fee fixed at award (16.304).

options.text: Firm-fixed-price (FFP)
options.why: Fixed-price family.

options.text: Indefinite-delivery
options.why: Indefinite-delivery is about quantity and timing; orders can be fixed-price or cost-type.

options.text: Time-and-materials (T&M)
options.why: T&M is its own category, neither fixed-price nor cost-reimbursement.

stem: You are buying software development where the requirements are not well defined and the scope may change. Which contract type fits best?

options.text: Cost-plus-fixed-fee (a cost-reimbursement type)
options.why: Cost-reimbursement fits when requirements cannot be defined well enough for fixed price, or uncertainties prevent a good cost estimate (16.301-2).

options.text: Firm-fixed-price with a detailed specification
options.why: FFP needs clearly defined requirements and a fair price you can set at the outset (16.202-2).

options.text: Time-and-materials
options.why: T&M is the least preferred type and gives the contractor no incentive to control costs.

options.text: Fixed-price with economic price adjustment
options.why: EPA handles unstable market prices, not undefined requirements.

stem: Which contract type carries the LOWEST cost risk for the contractor?

options.text: Cost-plus-fixed-fee
options.why: The Government reimburses allowable costs and the fee is fixed, so the contractor carries the least cost risk.

options.text: Firm-fixed-price
options.why: FFP puts the most cost risk on the contractor.

options.text: Fixed-price incentive (firm target)
options.why: The contractor shares cost overruns up to the ceiling price.

options.text: Fixed-price with economic price adjustment
options.why: Still fixed-price: the contractor carries cost risk except for the named market changes.

stem: What is the purpose of a performance work statement (PWS)?

options.text: To describe the required results and the standards the contractor must meet
options.why: A PWS states outcomes in measurable terms, leaving the how to the contractor (performance-based acquisition).

options.text: To list the technical specifications and the step-by-step methods the contractor must use
options.why: Detailed how-to specifications fit a SOW, not a PWS.

options.text: To set the evaluation criteria for the source selection
options.why: Evaluation criteria are in Section M.

options.text: To set the contract terms, conditions and clauses
options.why: Terms are in clauses.

stem: You must buy specialized equipment. Market research finds only two vendors that meet the technical requirements. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Document the market research and compete the requirement between them
options.why: Two capable sources mean competition is possible. Document the results in a way that suits the buy (10.001(e)).

options.text: Go sole source because there are only two capable vendors
options.why: Two sources can compete; sole source needs one source and a justification.

options.text: Cancel the requirement for lack of competition
options.why: Two sources are competition.

options.text: Solicit both vendors right away without documenting the market research results
options.why: Market research must be documented.

stem: What is the purpose of a sole-source justification?

options.text: To document why only one source can meet the need, citing the statutory authority
options.why: A justification must cite the authority and show why the source's unique qualifications or the nature of the buy require it (6.104-1(a)).

options.text: To ask a vendor for a lower price before negotiations begin
options.why: Pricing is negotiated, not justified.

options.text: To protest an award that went to another source
options.why: Protests are under Part 33.

options.text: To speed up the buy when the customer needs it quickly and cannot wait for competition
options.why: Speed alone is not a justification; lack of planning never is.

stem: How is a protest different from a claim?

options.text: A protest challenges a solicitation or award; a claim seeks relief under an existing contract
options.why: Protests are filed by interested parties about the buying process (33.102). Claims are written demands under a contract and follow the Disputes process (2.101, subpart 33.2).

options.text: They are the same thing, filed with different offices
options.why: Different parties, timing, forums and rules.

options.text: A protest is filed only after performance ends; a claim is filed before the contract is awarded
options.why: Protests concern solicitations and awards.

options.text: A claim is filed with GAO, and a protest goes to the contracting officer
options.why: Claims go to the contracting officer, then a board or the Court of Federal Claims.

stem: Under a proposal evaluation in Part 15, what is usually the first step after proposals arrive?

options.text: Evaluate each proposal against the requirements and the factors stated in the RFP
options.why: Evaluation assesses each proposal and the offeror's ability to perform, based solely on the RFP's factors (15.202(a)(1)).

options.text: Run a price analysis to find the lowest bidder and stop there
options.why: Price is evaluated along with the other factors, not alone.

options.text: Verify past performance before anything else, then look at the prices to rank them
options.why: Past performance is one factor in the evaluation, not a gate in front of it.

options.text: Hold negotiations with all offerors to clarify their proposals
options.why: Negotiations, if any, come after the competitive range is set.
